cases.title: Severity inflated to Extreme / Observed

agents_named.issue: Severity is overstated. CAP 'Extreme' means an extraordinary threat to life or property, and the headline says 'EXTREME DANGER'. The NCM bulletin describes fresh to strong winds with visibility below 2,000 m in some areas and only urges the public to exercise caution, especially when driving. That fits a possible threat (Moderate), not an extraordinary one.

Severity mismatch between the two headlines. The English opens with "EXTREME DANGER:" and the Arabic headline has no equivalent, so the two audiences receive different severity signals. The drafter cannot simply add or remove the label: the body text describes an advisory-level hazard (take extra care), so the English label itself may be wrong. A person must decide the intended severity.

objections.issue: Severity is overstated. CAP 'Extreme' means an extraordinary threat to life or property, and the headline says 'EXTREME DANGER'. The NCM bulletin describes fresh to strong winds with visibility below 2,000 m in some areas and only urges the public to exercise caution, especially when driving. That fits a possible threat (Moderate), not an extraordinary one.
objections.fix: Change severity from 'Extreme' to 'Moderate', which matches the bulletin's call for caution. Remove 'EXTREME DANGER' from the headline, for example: 'Dusty winds reducing visibility until 19:00 today'.

cases.title: Correction sent as a new alert with no reference

agents_named.issue: The alert tells the public to disregard the weather alert and that no action is needed. The verified NCM bulletin says blowing dust and reduced visibility are ongoing until 19:00 and urges caution. The alert therefore contradicts the verified hazard and could lead people to drop precautions during an active warning. Whether an earlier alert was actually erroneous cannot be confirmed from the inputs, so a person must decide.

The certainty, urgency and severity fields describe an observed, immediate hazard. The headline and description say the alert was sent in error. The alert therefore gives contradictory signals about whether the hazard exists.

The headline says this message corrects or withdraws an earlier alert, but msgType is 'Alert' and references is null, so it does not identify which alert it corrects. The system also shows no earlier alerts, so recipients cannot tell what to disregard.

reviews.name: Met office reviewer
reviews.summary: The verified NCM bulletin reports an active dust hazard from 14:55 to 19:00 on 4 March 2026. In that bulletin, NCM urges caution while driving. The alert instead tells the public to disregard an earlier alert and says no action is needed. This contradicts the verified hazard. The structured fields (Observed/Immediate/Moderate) also conflict with the retraction text. A person must decide whether an earlier message really was sent in error and should be cancelled. Either way, the alert must not tell the public that no action is needed while the NCM warning is in force. The unverified dam rumour is correctly left out.

objections.issue: The alert tells the public to disregard the weather alert and that no action is needed. The verified NCM bulletin says blowing dust and reduced visibility are ongoing until 19:00 and urges caution. The alert therefore contradicts the verified hazard and could lead people to drop precautions during an active warning. Whether an earlier alert was actually erroneous cannot be confirmed from the inputs, so a person must decide.

reviews.name: Network operator and regulator reviewer
reviews.summary: Both required languages (ar, en) are present. Each is under the 15-page maximum (en 3 pages, ar 6 pages). The encodings are correct: GSM-7 for English and UCS-2 for Arabic, which Arabic requires. However, neither language tells people what to do: the text gives the hazard (dust and sand, visibility under 2,000 m) and how long it lasts, but no protective action, so the first page cannot carry one. The drafter can fix this.

objections.issue: No protective action in either language. The English and Arabic texts describe only the hazard, the expected end time and the source, so the first page carries no action for the recipient.
objections.fix: Add a short protective action right after the hazard statement in both languages, before the time and source lines, so it lands on page 1. For example, EN: 'Drive with caution, keep a safe distance, and avoid outdoor activity if you have breathing problems.' Add the equivalent in AR. Then recheck the page counts, which should stay well under 15.

reviews.name: Arabic language reviewer
reviews.summary: The headline and description match: the hazard, northwesterly winds, visibility under 2,000 metres, coastal and inland areas, 19:00 on 4 March, and the source. The instruction does not. The English tells drivers no precautions are needed and to drive as normal. The machine-translated Arabic tells them to take extra care, especially on open roads, because visibility may drop. English and Arabic readers would get opposite protective actions. A person at the issuing authority must decide which action is intended before either text is aligned. A named Arabic reader must still approve the Arabic.

objections.issue: The protective action is reversed between languages. English: 'No special precautions are needed; drive as normal.' Arabic: 'Take extra care, especially when driving on open roads, as visibility may drop due to blowing dust.' Arabic readers would be told to act differently from English readers. This cannot be fixed by retranslating, because the English instruction itself sits oddly with a hazard that cuts visibility below 2,000 m. The issuing authority must decide the correct action; then both languages should be made to state it identically and be checked by a human Arabic reviewer.
objections.fix: Escalate to the issuing authority to confirm the intended protective action. Rewrite whichever language is wrong so both state the same action. Have a named Arabic reader approve the final Arabic instruction.

cases.title: Correction sent as a new alert with no reference

agents_named.issue: The description says an earlier alert was sent in error. No event input reports such an error. The verified NCM bulletin confirms a live fog hazard over this period, so the alert contradicts the bulletin and rests on an unverified claim.

The headline tells the public to disregard an earlier alert, but msgType is "Alert" and references is null. A correction must be a Cancel or Update that points to the message it corrects. No earlier alerts from this system exist, so it is unclear which alert is being retracted, and a stand-alone Actual alert like this could confuse the public.

reviews.name: Met office reviewer
reviews.summary: The alert tells the public to disregard an earlier weather alert as sent in error and says no action is needed. No input supports this. The only verified hazard input is an active NCM fog warning for western regions, 21:30 on 17 Feb to 10:00 on 18 Feb, with visibility possibly dropping to zero. A retraction would contradict the bulletin. Whether any earlier alert was truly erroneous, and whether a separate correct fog warning must go out, is for the issuing authority to decide.

objections.issue: The description says an earlier alert was sent in error. No event input reports such an error. The verified NCM bulletin confirms a live fog hazard over this period, so the alert contradicts the bulletin and rests on an unverified claim.
objections.fix: A person at the issuing authority must confirm whether an earlier alert was actually erroneous. If it was a genuine fog alert, do not retract it. Issue or keep a fog warning matching NCM: fog and reduced visibility, possibly zero, across several western regions, from 21:30 on 17 Feb until 10:00 on 18 Feb. If a true cancellation is needed, it must reference the specific erroneous message as a Cancel and must not imply the NCM fog hazard is void.

reviews.summary: The Arabic matches the English in meaning across all three fields. The headline "تجاهلوا التنبيه السابق" means "Disregard the earlier alert". reviews.name: Issuing authority reviewer
reviews.summary: The alert is an Actual, public alert in a live console for a real event, but its sender, unknown-sender@nadhir.example, is not in the issuer register. The only registered issuer is demo-national-authority@nadhir.example. Only an authorised entity may send warning messages, and the drafter cannot fix this by swapping in another identity, so a person must decide whether this originator may issue. All other checks pass: the area matches the area drawn for event uae-fog-2026-02-17, there are no active alerts from higher authorities, and msgType Alert needs no references.

objections.issue: The sender is not in the issuer register. The register lists only demo-national-authority@nadhir.example, so this originator has no authorisation for any area or category. Sending warnings is limited to authorised entities, and this alert would go out live as Actual.
objections.fix: A person must confirm the originator's authority. Either the alert is re-issued under a sender listed in the issuer register, with that issuer's approval, or the sender is formally added to the register before release.

reviews.summary: Both required languages (ar, en) are present. Encodings are correct: GSM-7 for English and UCS-2 for Arabic. Page counts (3 and 6) are within the 15-page cell broadcast maximum. However, neither language tells people what to do. The first page names the fog hazard but carries no protective action, and there is no action anywhere in the message. The drafter can fix this.

objections.issue: No protective action in either language. Both the English and Arabic texts describe the fog hazard, area, time and source, but never tell recipients what to do. The first page therefore carries the hazard but not the action.
objections.fix: Add a short protective action right after the hazard in both languages, so it falls on the first page. For example, English: 'Fog warning: thick fog, visibility near zero in western UAE. Drive slowly, use low-beam lights, keep a safe distance.' Arabic equivalent: 'تحذير من الضباب: قلّل السرعة واستخدم الأضواء المنخفضة.' Then the area, timing and source details. Keep Arabic within 15 pages at 41 UCS-2 characters a page.

reviews.summary: The hazard, visibility threshold (under 3,000 m), wind description, end time (18:00), severity (Moderate), certainty (Observed) and urgency (Immediate) all match the verified NCM bulletin, and nothing unverified is used. One place issue: the bulletin warns of 'some coastal and inland areas' nationally, while the alert ties them to 'Abu Dhabi (demo zone)'. objections.fix: Describe the area as the bulletin does: 'some coastal and inland areas'. If a demo zone label is needed for the exercise, keep it clearly separate and do not present Abu Dhabi as the hazard area.

reviews.summary: Both required languages (ar, en) are present, the encoding is correct (GSM-7 for English, UCS-2 for Arabic), and page counts (3 and 5) are within the 15-page cell broadcast maximum. Keep the hazard at the start and recheck that page counts stay within 15.

cases.title: 'This is not a drill' inside a drill

agents_named.issue: The description ends with 'This is not a drill.' The event context and the alert status both mark this as an exercise, and no input supports presenting it as a real event. In an Exercise message this sentence could lead the public to treat a drill as a live warning.

The text is marked EXERCISE / تمرين and refers to a demo zone, yet ends with 'This is not a drill.' / 'هذا ليس تمريناً.' A reader on a handset gets contradictory signals about whether the alert is real.

The Arabic, like the English, contradicts itself on whether the alert is real. It opens with 'تمرين' (exercise) and ends with 'هذا ليس تمريناً' (this is not an exercise/drill). The translation is faithful, but Arabic readers cannot tell whether to act. Mixing exercise labels with 'this is not a drill' contributed to the Hawaii false alert. Whether this is an exercise or a live alert is a decision for a person, not the translator.

reviews.name: Met office reviewer
reviews.summary: The hazard, end time (18:00), visibility threshold, severity (Moderate), urgency and certainty (Observed, conditions began 10:30) all match the NCM bulletin. Two problems need fixing. The description says 'This is not a drill', which contradicts the exercise context. It also ties the affected areas to Abu Dhabi, which the bulletin does not do.

objections.issue: The description ends with 'This is not a drill.' The event context and the alert status both mark this as an exercise, and no input supports presenting it as a real event. In an Exercise message this sentence could lead the public to treat a drill as a live warning.
objections.fix: Delete 'This is not a drill.' If a closing line is wanted, use something like 'This is an exercise message only.'

However, both texts label the message 'EXERCISE' and also say 'This is not a drill.' The Arabic reproduces this exactly ('تمرين' and 'هذا ليس تمريناً'), so Arabic readers get the same contradiction. A person must decide whether this is an exercise or a live alert before the wording can be fixed in both languages. The Arabic is machine-translated and still needs sign-off by a named Arabic reader.

objections.issue: The Arabic, like the English, contradicts itself on whether the alert is real. It opens with 'تمرين' (exercise) and ends with 'هذا ليس تمريناً' (this is not an exercise/drill). The translation is faithful, but Arabic readers cannot tell whether to act. Mixing exercise labels with 'this is not a drill' contributed to the Hawaii false alert. Whether this is an exercise or a live alert is a decision for a person, not the translator.
objections.fix: The issuing authority must decide whether this is an exercise or live. If it is an exercise, remove 'This is not a drill.' and 'هذا ليس تمريناً.' If it is live, remove the 'EXERCISE'/'تمرين' labels. Then re-check the Arabic against the corrected English.

objections.issue: The place wording is broader than the bulletin. The NCM bulletin covers 'several western regions of the UAE'. The alert says 'across western regions', and the description calls the fog 'thick', which implies a wider and firmer hazard than the bulletin's 'potential fog formation'. The bulletin mentions thick fog only in its safety advice, as 'areas experiencing thick fog'.
objections.fix: Reword to match the bulletin, for example: 'Fog may form and visibility may drop to zero at times across several western regions of the UAE, from 21:30 tonight (Tue 17 Feb) until 10:00 Wed 18 Feb.' Use 'several western regions' in the headline too.

objections.issue: No protective action appears anywhere in either language, so the first page carries the hazard but not the action. The alert only describes the fog and its timing, and never says what people should do (for example, avoid unnecessary travel, drive slowly with low-beam lights, keep a safe distance). The CAP guidance expects people to act on the guidance the alert provides.
objections.fix: Add a short protective action in both English and Arabic, placed right after the hazard so it falls on the first page. For example: 'Fog warning: zero visibility possible in western UAE. Avoid travel; if driving, slow down, use low beams, keep distance.' Then give the times and source. In Arabic, keep the hazard and action within the first 41-character page as far as possible, e.g. 'ضباب كثيف: تجنب القيادة، وإن اضطررت فخفف السرعة' followed by details. Keep each language at 15 pages or fewer.
